Strategic Asphyxiation: The U.S. Approach to Iran 
Pressure by a thousand cuts

The strategic asphyxiation strategy has four defining features:

Economic constriction: Reduce the revenues and access to foreign currency that finance the wider system. Operation Economic Outcast targets this layer through oil exports, trade, financial intermediaries, and sanctions-evasion mechanisms.

Network disruption: Target the IRGC financial, procurement, shipping, and logistical networks that convert money into technology, components, weapons, and support abroad. Economic pressure has a limited effect if Tehran can still move resources through alternative channels.

Industrial degradation: Damage the military infrastructure that converts technology and materiel into missiles, drones, and other weapons. Strikes on production facilities make losses harder and more expensive to replace.

Regional attrition: Increase the cost of Iran’s external commitments by weakening the armed groups and supply networks through which Tehran projects power. Pressure in Iraq, Yemen, Lebanon, and elsewhere forces Iran to spend increasingly constrained resources defending investments accumulated over decades.

Washington still has work to do, but sustained strategic asphyxiation will sooner or later force the Islamic Republic to confront a fundamental choice: abandon the revolutionary ambitions that have cost Iran and its people billions of dollars, or pursue them at an increasingly unbearable price until the revolution itself consumes what remains of the regime.

and ultimately this will be a good thing. the learning curve just hurts

#Uranium #Silver #Copper #Gold

⚡ DAILY METALS PULSE — OCTOBER 12, 2026
Monday evening update
A firmer dollar and rising oil pressured precious metals today, while nuclear fuel investment and copper security stayed in focus.

☢️ URANIUM
Today’s World Nuclear News coverage highlighted Urenco USA’s sixth new enrichment cascade entering production. Its current eight-cascade expansion is now 75% complete, with the final cascade expected in spring 2027.

My takeaway: rebuilding Western nuclear fuel capacity is progressing. Securing reliable uranium feedstock remains an essential part of that effort.

🥈 SILVER
New York silver futures finished around $60.14/oz, down 0.9%. A difficult start to the week as the dollar strengthened and energy inflation concerns weighed on precious metals.

Watching whether silver can hold its ground ahead of Wednesday’s US CPI.

🔩 COPPER
Today’s Reuters analysis put US copper inventories at roughly 1.1 million tonnes, following inflows encouraged by the premium in US futures prices.
These are predominantly commercial holdings. Their location could change if the price incentives reverse, making trade policy and regional availability key issues to watch.

🥇 GOLD
Front-month COMEX gold settled at $4,165.80/oz, down 0.6%. Dollar strength and higher oil prices kept investors focused on the risk of persistent inflation and tighter Fed policy.

📌 NEXT UP
Canadian mining stocks return Tuesday after Thanksgiving. US CPI follows Wednesday, then PPI and retail sales Thursday.
My focus: uranium fuel developments, copper inventory flows, and whether gold and silver find support before the inflation releases. ⚒️

Gold around $4,171 after retreating from an early one-week high. The dollar is keeping pressure on bullion ahead of CPI Wednesday, followed by PPI and retail sales Thursday.

📌 WEEK AHEAD
Inflation data, the dollar, Chilean mine developments and follow-through in uranium equities.
TSX and TSXV are closed today for Canadian Thanksgiving, so Canadian mining stocks rejoin the action Tuesday.

My focus: how the metals respond to the data—and whether miners confirm the move. ⚒️

Jason Calacanis: AI is the End of Coding as We Know It

“People were lamenting how something has been lost in developing code because coders used to work together to solve a problem, and there was this esprit de corps, there was this camaraderie in building towards a goal.

And now they're not working with each other, they're working with agents. They're not actually constructing the code. They're only reviewing 10-15% of it now, which means they're going to be reviewing none of it very shortly.

And that the whole joy of building as a coder was basically going away.

Their way of life, of building this building together, known as software, was now being deprecated. It was going away.

And it seems to be a paradigm shift in which they're not solving the problem, they're constructing the problem set and handing it off to AI.”
